title: What a Parent Should Actually Listen For in a Child's First Year of Piano
description: Most parents judge progress by how many pieces their child can play. A concert pianist and university teacher explains the four things worth listening for instead, and the one that predicts whether a child keeps going.
sub: Parents ask me whether their child is doing well. The honest answer has almost nothing to do with how many pieces they can play, and everything to do with four quieter things.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: The free course is written for adults, but the ear work in Lesson 1 is the same at any age:
body:
A parent asked me last year whether her daughter was behind. The other child in their class had learned six pieces that term; hers had learned three. I asked her to play me both. The girl who had learned three was the one I would have bet on, and I want to explain why, because the thing parents are given to measure is almost never the thing that matters.

Pieces learned is a countable number, and countable numbers are comforting. But a piece can be learned by understanding it or by memorising the sequence of finger movements that produce it, and from the outside those two look identical for about a year. Then they stop looking identical, sharply, and the child who memorised movements hits a wall that nobody can explain to them.

Here is what I listen for instead.

1. Can they find a tune by ear?

Ask your child to play Happy Birthday, or anything they know, without music in front of them. Not well — just to find it, slowly, hunting for the next note and correcting themselves when it is wrong.

A child who can do this has connected the sound in their head to the keys under their hand. That connection is the whole instrument. A child who cannot, after a year of lessons, has been taught to convert symbols into finger movements without the sound ever passing through, and that is the most common and most damaging gap in beginner teaching.

It is also completely fixable, at any point, by asking for it. Children find tunes by ear readily when someone tells them it is allowed.

2. Do they play the same phrase twice in a row the same way?

Not the same as the recording. The same as themselves, twice.

Consistency means the child has a mental model of the passage. Inconsistency — a different note wrong each time, a different hesitation — means they are reconstructing it from scratch on every attempt, which is exhausting and does not accumulate. This is the single most useful thing a non-musician parent can notice, because it needs no musical knowledge at all. You are simply listening for whether it is the same twice.

3. What does their hand look like when they are concentrating?

Watch the moment the music gets harder. Do the fingers flatten out? Do the shoulders rise? Does the wrist drop below the level of the keys?

Everyone tenses under difficulty; that is not the problem. The question is whether the tension releases afterwards or whether it has become the default posture. A child who plays with raised shoulders in month two and still does in month ten has learned the tension along with the notes, and it will cost them years later. Say nothing in the moment — corrections during playing rarely land — but mention it to the teacher.

4. Do they ever play when nobody asked them to?

This is the one that predicts whether they continue.

Not practice. Practice is a duty and duties are negotiated. I mean the five minutes of aimless noise on the way past the instrument — picking out a film theme, banging out something they invented, playing the same four bars eleven times because they like how it sounds. That is a child who has understood that the piano is theirs to use rather than a subject they are being tested on.

If it never happens, the instrument has become homework. That is worth addressing directly, and usually the fix is not more discipline but less: a stretch of time where nothing is being assessed and they are allowed to make a mess.

What I would stop measuring

Speed. Fast playing is a by-product of secure playing, never a route to it. A child pushed to play faster learns to push, and pushing is the habit that has to be undone first in every adult I have ever retaught.

Comparisons with the other child in the class. Children arrive with different amounts of music already in their ears, and that gap closes. What does not close on its own is a missing connection between sound and key.

Grade exams, in the first year. They are a useful external deadline later. Early on they tend to produce three very well-drilled pieces and nothing underneath them.

The question to ask the teacher

Not “how is she doing”, which invites a polite answer. Ask: what is the one thing you are working on with her at the moment, and how will I know when it is solved?

A teacher with a plan answers that immediately and specifically. A teacher without one gives you a general impression. You will learn more from thirty seconds of that answer than from a term of reports.

One last thing

Almost every adult who comes to me having “played as a child and given it up” describes the same ending: it stopped being interesting, and nobody noticed in time. Very few of them stopped because it was too hard.

So if you are going to watch one thing, watch the fourth one. A child who plays when nobody asked is a child who is going to keep playing.

title: Learning Piano After 70: What Changes, What Does Not
description: An honest account of what is genuinely different about starting piano in your seventies, what is not different at all, and how to design practice around the parts that are.
sub: Some things really are different, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. Most of the important ones are not, and that is the part people are not told.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko seated at the piano
cta_text: The free course starts from nothing and moves one page at a time:
body:
I teach people in their seventies and eighties. It goes well, routinely, and I want to be precise about why rather than encouraging, because encouragement without detail is not much use to anyone.

Let me start with what is actually different.

What changes

How long a new physical habit takes to settle. A movement that a twenty-year-old owns after three days may take a week or two. This is a difference in rate, not in outcome — the habit forms, and once formed it is as reliable as anyone's. What it means practically is that the number of repetitions matters more than the length of the session, so short daily practice beats long occasional practice by a wider margin than it does for a younger beginner.

Reading small print on a page at arm's length. This is the most common real obstacle and it is almost always mistaken for a musical difficulty. If the notes are a struggle to see, everything downstream — rhythm, hand position, confidence — degrades, and the student concludes they cannot read music. Enlarge the score. Most editions can be photocopied larger, many are available in large print, and reading on a tablet lets you set the size yourself. I have watched this one change transform a student's playing in a fortnight, and it has nothing to do with music.

Stiffness first thing. Hands that have been still are not ready to play. A short warm-up matters more than it does at thirty — a minute of slow movement before the first piece rather than starting cold. If something hurts, that is a question for your doctor and not for a piano teacher, and I say that plainly: pain is information, and it is not the kind I am qualified to interpret.

How many things you can hold at once while playing. Sight-reading a new piece while also counting aloud while also watching your hand is a lot to run at the same time, for anyone, and the margin narrows with age. The answer is not to try harder. It is to do those things one at a time and then put them together, which is what good practice looks like at any age and merely becomes non-optional here.

What does not change

Your ear. Seventy years of listening is seventy years of musical understanding that a ten-year-old does not have. You know when a phrase has ended. You know when something sounds unresolved. You have opinions about tempo. Children acquire that slowly and you already own it, and it is by a distance the largest single advantage anyone brings to the instrument.

Your ability to understand an explanation. I can tell an adult why the arm delivers weight and the finger only directs it, and they can apply it the same afternoon. With a child I demonstrate the same idea for a year.

Your capacity to learn to read music. There is nothing about reading notation that requires a young brain. It requires repeated exposure, which requires the notes to be legible, which returns us to the point about print size.

Whether the result is worth listening to. This is the one people quietly doubt, and it is the one I am most confident about. The playing of an older beginner who works sensibly is frequently more musical than that of a faster younger one, because musicality is mostly judgement, and judgement is the thing you have most of.

How I would design the practice

Fifteen or twenty minutes, most days, rather than an hour twice a week. This is the single highest-value structural decision, and it matters more here than at any other age.

Warm up before the music, always. A minute. Slow movement, hands separately, nothing you have to read.

Enlarge everything. Score, and the light on the music desk. Then judge your reading.

Hands separately for longer than you think is necessary. Not because the coordination will not come, but because putting hands together prematurely is where the tension gets learned, and unlearning tension is the slow part.

Pick music you actually want to hear. Nobody at seventy is building a career, which means the only reason to spend the time is that the sound is worth having in the room. That is a better reason than most people practise for, and it tends to produce better practice.

The thing that stops people, and it is not what they think

In my experience older beginners almost never stop because it was too difficult. They stop because they decided in advance how fast it should go, measured themselves against that, and concluded they were failing.

So set the expectation properly at the start. In the first year you can reasonably expect to read simple music in both hands, play pieces you recognise, and understand what you are doing rather than copying it. That is a realistic year, it is a substantial one, and it is available.

The free course begins at the beginning and moves one page at a time. And if you would like me to tell you what I actually hear, you can send me a recording — it is free while the feedback pilot runs.

title: The Plateau: Why Month Four Feels Like Going Backwards
description: Nearly every adult beginner hits a stretch where progress seems to stop or reverse. What is actually happening, why it arrives at roughly the same point for everybody, and what to change.
sub: It arrives at around the same time for almost everyone, it feels like proof that you have no talent, and it is in fact a specific and well-understood thing.
image_alt: The strings inside a grand piano
cta_text: If you are in the middle of one, the lessons are free and you can go back a few:
body:
Somewhere around the third or fourth month, most adult beginners write to me with the same message in different words: it was going well, and now it has stopped. Pieces that were coming together have fallen apart. Things I could do last month I cannot do this month. Perhaps this was always going to happen.

It is so consistent that I now mention it in advance, because knowing what it is removes most of its force.

What is actually happening

Three things arrive at once, and they arrive together for structural reasons.

Your ear has improved faster than your hands. This is the main one. Three months of concentrated listening sharpens your judgement considerably, and judgement improves faster than physical skill does. So you are now hearing faults that were always there and that you previously could not detect. The playing has not got worse. The listener has got better, and the listener is you. This is genuinely good news wearing an unpleasant disguise.

The easy gains are spent. The first weeks contain a run of large, visible wins: the first time both hands work together, the first recognisable tune. Those are step changes and they run out. What follows is the same rate of real progress spread over smaller, less visible increments — which feels like stopping even though nothing has stopped.

The music has started to require two things at once. Around here, pieces begin asking you to read, keep time, and control the sound simultaneously. Each was manageable alone. Together they exceed what you can currently run in parallel, so the whole performance degrades and it looks like a loss of ability. It is a load problem.

What to change

Take the load apart. If three things at once is too much, do them one at a time on purpose. Clap and count the rhythm with no keyboard at all. Play the notes with no rhythm, just finding them. Then play slowly enough that all of it fits. Slow is not a lesser version of the piece; slow is the speed at which you can still control it, and that speed rises on its own.

Go back to something from month one and play it. This is the most useful thing on this list and the one people resist hardest, because it feels like retreating. Do it anyway. You will find it easy in a way it was not, and that is the objective evidence your ear is currently refusing to supply. It also gives you the sensation of playing well, which you have not had for a few weeks and which is the actual fuel here.

Record yourself, once, and put it beside a recording from two months ago. Memory is not a reliable instrument for this. A recording is. Most people are surprised, and the surprise is what breaks the mood.

Shorten the sessions. A discouraged person practising for an hour is mostly rehearsing discouragement. Twenty focused minutes is better in every respect.

Change one thing about the material. A different key, a piece from outside the book, a tune you find by ear. The plateau is partly attentional, and novelty restores attention.

What not to do

Do not practise more. More repetitions of an unsolved problem install the problem more firmly. This is the reflex, and it is wrong.

Do not add a harder piece to prove something. It will confirm the fear rather than dispel it.

Do not decide anything about your talent this month. You are making a judgement about a long-term prospect using data from the single least representative period in it.

How long it lasts

I will not give you a number, because it varies with what you do about it and I do not invent figures. What I will say is that it ends, that the ending is usually not dramatic, and that in retrospect nearly everyone describes this stretch as the point where their playing actually became musical — because it is where you stopped hitting notes and started listening to them.

The lessons are free and they stay up, so going back three of them costs nothing. And if you want to know whether what you are hearing is real, send me a recording — feedback is free while the pilot runs, and this is precisely the question it is good at answering.

title: Why You Freeze When Someone Listens
description: A concert pianist on what actually happens when you play in front of another person, why your hands stop working, and the practical things that help.
sub: You have played it forty times alone and it was fine. Someone walks into the room and your hands are suddenly not yours. There are reasons, and there are things that work.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko in concert dress at the piano
cta_text: Everything in the free course is designed to be played alone first:
body:
I have walked onto concert platforms for most of my life and I still know exactly the sensation an adult beginner describes when their partner comes into the room. It does not go away with experience. What changes is what you do with it, and that part is learnable.

First, what is actually going wrong, because the usual explanation — nerves — is too vague to act on.

The piece was never as secure as it felt

This is the largest single cause and the least welcome.

Playing alone, you are running on a chain of physical habit: each movement cues the next. It is smooth and it feels like knowing the piece. It is not the same as knowing the piece. Break the chain anywhere — and attention on you is precisely what breaks it — and there is nothing underneath to fall back on, because you never needed anything underneath.

The test: start from the middle. Open the music at bar seventeen and begin there. If you cannot, you have a chain rather than a piece, and that is what collapses in company. The fix is to practise starting from four or five different points, so that a break drops you onto solid ground instead of into nothing.

You are listening to yourself differently

Alone, you listen to the music. With someone there, you listen to yourself being heard — monitoring, judging, predicting their reaction. That is a second task running alongside the playing, and it takes capacity from exactly the place the playing needs it.

The only thing I have found that genuinely helps is giving your attention a specific job it cannot do while it is monitoring. Not “relax” — that is not a task. Something concrete: make the left hand quieter than the right in this section. Listen for the last note of each phrase. Attention will go somewhere; decide where.

The tempo runs away

Almost everyone plays faster in front of people, without noticing, and the faster tempo is what causes the mistakes that are then blamed on nerves.

Set the first phrase deliberately slower than feels right. You will not sound slow; you will sound composed. The rate at which you play the opening bar effectively decides the rest.

The breathing stops

Watch yourself at the difficult bar and you will find you are holding your breath. A held breath stiffens the shoulders, a stiff shoulder cannot deliver weight, and a hand that cannot get weight from the arm compensates by gripping. That whole chain starts with the breath.

Mark two or three places in the score where you will exhale — actually mark them, in pencil — and practise breathing there until it is as automatic as the fingering. This is the oldest trick in the profession and the most reliable.

What to do in the week before

Play it once a day at the wrong time. Cold, first thing, without a warm-up, without a run-through. Performance is a cold start and practising only warm is practising the wrong conditions.

Record yourself. A running camera produces a surprising amount of the same self-consciousness, and it is the cheapest rehearsal for it available.

Play it for one safe person. One is the step. The gap between nobody and one person is far larger than the gap between one and twenty.

Decide in advance what you do when you stumble. This is the part people skip. If you have no plan, you will stop and apologise. If you have decided — carry on from the next phrase, no comment, no expression — you will do that instead, and the listener will very often not have noticed anything.

The thing nobody tells beginners

The people listening to you are not assessing you. They cannot hear the wrong note in bar twelve; they hear whether the music went somewhere. A performance with three errors and a shape is a good performance. A flawless one with no direction is not, and every musician knows it.

That is not consolation. It is the actual standard, and playing to it rather than to an imagined error count is what eventually makes playing for people enjoyable.

If you would like to practise being heard by one person who is not going to be startled by anything, send me a recording. Feedback is free while the pilot runs, and this is a reasonable and quite common reason to use it.

title: What Should Actually Happen in a Piano Lesson
description: What a well-run piano lesson contains, what a poorly-run one looks like, and how an adult can tell the difference from inside the room after four weeks.
sub: Most adults have never seen a good lesson and so have nothing to compare theirs with. Here is what the hour is supposed to contain.
cta_text: The free course is built on the same structure, lesson by lesson:
body:
Adults are strikingly bad at judging their own lessons, and it is not their fault: they have nothing to compare against. A lesson where the teacher is friendly and the hour passes pleasantly feels like a good lesson. Sometimes it is. Often it is an hour of supervised practice, which is a different and much less valuable thing.

So here is what I think the hour should contain. Not a rigid order — a set of things that should all be somewhere in it.

1. Something is diagnosed

The teacher should, at some point, tell you what is wrong. Specifically: not “that was a bit uneven” but the fourth finger is arriving late because the hand is turning towards the thumb, and here is where you can hear it.

A diagnosis has three parts — what is happening, why, and where in the music you can hear it. If you leave your lessons knowing that things could be better but not what specifically to change, you are being assessed rather than taught, and that is the commonest failure in the trade.

2. Something is fixed in the room

Not assigned to be fixed at home. Fixed, while the teacher is watching, so that you have physically felt the correct version at least once.

This matters because you cannot reproduce at home a sensation you have never had. A student sent away to “work on evenness” will practise their existing habit more thoroughly. A student who has felt the even version four times under supervision has something to aim at.

3. You are told how to practise it, not just what to practise

“Practise bars 9 to 16” is not an instruction, it is a location. The instruction is the method: hands separately at this speed, then this rhythm variant, then together but only the first half, and here is how you will know it has worked.

Ask for this explicitly if it is not offered. It is the difference between a week of useful practice and a week of repetition.

4. You play something all the way through

A lesson consisting entirely of corrected fragments produces a student who can play no piece from start to finish. Some part of the hour should be uninterrupted playing, with the teacher listening and saying nothing until the end.

This is also the only way either of you finds out whether the piece actually holds together.

5. Something is heard, not just played

Somewhere in the hour the teacher should play, and you should listen — a phrase, a demonstration of two ways of doing the same bar. Description has limits. A sound has none.

This is the part most commonly missing in online teaching, and it is worth asking for.

6. You leave knowing the one thing

If you are given nine corrections you will carry out none. A good lesson ends with one priority, said plainly, that everything else waits behind.

If your teacher does not do this, do it yourself on the way home: decide which single thing you are taking. You will make more progress on one than on nine.

Signs the lesson is not working

You play, the teacher says “good, now the next one”, repeatedly. That is an audit of your homework, not teaching.

The same fault is mentioned every week for two months. Mentioning is not fixing. If it has not moved, the approach needs to change — and that is the teacher's job to notice, not yours.

You are never told why. Adults learn through understanding; a teacher who will not explain the mechanism is teaching you as though you were seven.

Nothing is ever taken away from you. Good teaching removes things — a piece that is too hard, a habit, an unnecessary movement. A lesson that only adds material is not being steered.

What is reasonable to ask for

All of this is reasonable to ask for directly, and most teachers will respond well to being asked. A useful sentence: what is the one thing you want me to change this week, and how will I know when I have?

If you are learning alone, you are your own teacher for all six of these, which is harder but not impossible — the six give you a checklist for your own practice. The one thing you cannot reliably do alone is the first: diagnose what is going wrong. That is what the free feedback is for. Send a recording and I will tell you what I hear.

title: Adults Learn Piano Differently From Children — and Mostly Better
description: The real differences between how an adult and a child learn the piano, which of them are disadvantages, which are advantages, and how to teach yourself accordingly.
sub: The comparison is always made in one direction. Having taught both for years, I think the balance is considerably more even than adults are told.
image_alt: Dr. Maria Pisarenko at the piano
cta_text: The free course is written for adults on exactly these grounds:
body:
“Children learn faster.” Every adult beginner has heard this and most believe it. Having taught both for years, I think it is half true in a way that hides something more useful.

Let me separate the parts.

Where children have the advantage

They acquire physical habits with less resistance. A child shown a hand position adopts it. An adult shown the same hand position analyses it, compares it with what they were doing, and then adopts a compromise. The analysis is useful for almost everything else and is a genuine obstacle here.

They are not embarrassed. A seven-year-old will play something badly in front of you with no distress at all. This is worth more than it sounds: it means they get many more low-stakes repetitions in a teacher's hearing, which means faults are caught early. Adults hide the bad attempts, and the bad attempts are the informative ones.

They have no deadline. Nobody has told a child they should be able to play something by Christmas. Adults set themselves schedules and then interpret the schedule as a verdict.

Where adults have the advantage — and it is a longer list

You can be told why. This is the big one. I can explain to an adult that the hammer is thrown at the string and then flies free, so that only the speed of the key changes the sound, so that pressing harder is physically incapable of producing a bigger tone. An adult hears that once and reorganises their arm the same afternoon. With a child I demonstrate the same idea for a year and hope.

Your ear is decades ahead. You have heard thousands of hours of music. You know when a phrase is finished, when something is out of tune, when a tempo is wrong. That is musicianship, it is the hardest thing to teach, and you already have it. Children build it slowly while their fingers race ahead — which is exactly why so many technically fluent children play unmusically.

You can diagnose your own practice. An adult can notice that bar eleven fails four times out of five, isolate it, work out that it is the hand shift and not the notes, and design a fix. A child cannot do this at all and does not learn to for years. It is the single most valuable skill in learning an instrument and adults arrive with it.

You chose this. Nobody drove you here. Motivation that comes from inside survives the difficult months that motivation from a parent does not.

You can concentrate for longer. Twenty focused adult minutes will beat forty supervised child minutes, most days.

What this means for how you should practise

Play to the advantages instead of imitating a children's method.

Ask for the mechanism, always. Never accept “just do it like this” if you can get “do it like this because”. Your comprehension is your fastest route and a method that does not use it is wasting you.

Use your ear first. Find tunes by ear before you read them. Hum a line before you play it. The Russian school begins here for children for a reason, and for an adult it is not a beginner's exercise — it is playing to your strongest card.

Be deliberate about the physical habits, because that is your weak side. Slower, fewer things at once, more repetitions of the movement alone without the music. The part that is genuinely harder for you is the part to give the structured time to.

Make the bad attempts in front of someone. Record them. Send them. This is the child's advantage you can most easily take back, and it costs only a little discomfort.

Do not set a date. Set a next thing instead.

The comparison that actually matters

An adult beginner is not competing with children. They are competing with the version of themselves that does not start.

And on the only question that finally matters — can you end up playing music that is worth listening to, including to yourself — I have never once seen age be the deciding factor. Practice design decides it, and practice design is a thing adults are good at.

The free course is written on these assumptions: it explains rather than instructs, it begins with the ear, and it takes the physical side slowly. And if you would like to know what an experienced listener actually hears in your playing, send a recording — it is free while the pilot runs.
